facts.text: Rome's historic center is compact and best done on foot; the metro has only two main lines and doesn't reach many central sights directly because of archaeological restrictions on digging.
A "coperto" (cover charge, roughly €1-3/person) is standard and legal at sit-down restaurants; it's not a scam, but an additional service charge stacked on top of it at touristy spots can be.

Restaurants with hosts aggressively inviting you in from the street, especially around Trevi Fountain, Piazza Navona, and right beside the Colosseum, are reliably tourist-priced with mediocre food — a few streets away (Trastevere, Monti) tends to be both cheaper and better.
The Colosseum, Roman Forum, and Palatine Hill share one ticket; booking a timed-entry slot in advance avoids the worst of the entry queue, especially in summer.
Many churches and some sights enforce a dress code (shoulders and knees covered) — this applies even in summer heat and is strictly enforced at St. Peter's Basilica.

Roman cuisine is meat/dairy-heavy (carbonara, cacio e pepe, amatriciana, saltimbocca) — vegetarian options exist but require more deliberate seeking outside the Jewish-Roman (Ghetto) area and modern trattorias.
Tap water ("acqua del rubinetto") is safe and free to request in restaurants; bottled water is often pushed by default and adds several euros per meal if you don't specify.
